part_title: X-Ray Tracing, Service Maps and AI Request Diagnostics

scenes.title: X-Ray Distributed Tracing for GenAI
scenes.narration: Follow this trace from the client across API Gateway, Lambda, Bedrock and the data services. The same trace identifier connects the pieces into one request path. Beneath each service, the slide breaks activity into segments and smaller subsegments: receiving the request, Lambda initialization, retrieving context, constructing the prompt, invoking the model and storing results. Now look at the measured durations. API Gateway is relatively brief, while Lambda's overall span includes a large Bedrock model invocation; the model-processing portion dominates the example. Be careful when reading the bars: some service durations overlap because a parent segment includes downstream work. Adding every segment duration together can double-count time. The end-to-end figure at the bottom represents the client experience, while subsegments explain where that time went. For a slow GenAI answer, X-Ray helps distinguish a cold start from retrieval latency and inference latency. Instrument the application, propagate trace context through supported calls and include safe request identifiers. This slide teaches a troubleshooting method, not just a service diagram: locate the longest critical path before changing compute sizes or model settings.

scenes.title: X-Ray Service Map
scenes.narration: This service map is a dependency graph you can use to find performance and reliability problems. Begin at the client and API Gateway nodes, then follow the arrows into Lambda and the downstream services. Each node shows traffic volume, response latency and an error rate. The legend indicates which latency ranges are healthy, elevated or a bottleneck. The example Lambda path shows an elevated latency and around three and a half percent errors, while the Bedrock dependency has around four point one percent errors. S3 and DynamoDB show lower latencies and error rates. The key is to look at dependency context rather than blaming the first service with a warning colour. Lambda's slow response may be caused largely by the model call it is waiting for. Compare request counts as well: a slow service carrying thousands of requests has more user impact than a rare background path. Use the service map to identify suspicious nodes, then open individual traces to confirm the source of delay or failure. A service map highlights where to investigate; it doesn't independently tell you why a model request failed.

scenes.title: X-Ray trace analysis
scenes.narration: Here we zoom from a service map into one slow request. Read the timeline from left to right: API Gateway receives and routes the request, Lambda has a cold-start phase, retrieval gathers relevant context, the model generates its answer, and post-processing formats the final response. The example request takes twelve point four three seconds. Look at the labelled durations: the cold start costs about one point eight four seconds, retrieval about one point one two seconds, and the model invocation about eight point six four seconds. The model stage is therefore the largest contributor, roughly seventy percent of total response time. The recommendation panel on the right suggests choosing a faster model when quality allows, shortening unnecessary prompt context and considering streaming to improve perceived responsiveness. Provisioned options may help specific capacity needs, but must be evaluated for availability and cost. Streaming often improves time to first token without necessarily shortening total generation time. The diagnostic lesson is to optimise the largest measured contributor before making unrelated changes. X-Ray reveals where the time went; model quality tests tell you whether the optimisation is acceptable.

scenes.title: X-Ray annotations and metadata
scenes.narration: This slide separates two types of trace context. Annotations are searchable attributes, such as environment, model ID, tenant category and request type. In the example, a production RAG request includes these fields so operators can filter traces by deployment or model. Metadata contains richer operational details such as prompt-token count, completion-token count, number of retrieved documents, measured latency and estimated request cost. The JSON panel shows how these two categories appear in a trace record. Why does the distinction matter? You can index and search annotations efficiently, while metadata is primarily for examining details after opening a trace. Now read the privacy section at the bottom. Replace personal identifiers with approved redacted or pseudonymous values, avoid storing full prompts and retrieved documents, and restrict access to trace data. Operational fields can still be sensitive if they identify a tenant or user. The right balance is enough context to compare performance and debug failures without copying private customer content into every trace. Choose a small, consistent set of searchable annotations and put only necessary troubleshooting details in metadata.

scenes.title: Debug a Failed AI Request with Logs and Traces
scenes.narration: This slide provides a five-step investigation of a failed model request. First, the application captures a trace ID and request ID when the user asks to summarise a document. Second, search CloudWatch logs for those identifiers. The example error line reports a Bedrock InvokeModel failure. Third, open the matching X-Ray trace to follow the path through API Gateway, Lambda and the Bedrock call. Fourth, inspect the error details: the response is HTTP four twenty-nine with ThrottlingException, meaning the model request rate exceeded an allowed limit. Finally, choose the retry policy based on the error class. For throttling or temporary unavailability, apply bounded exponential backoff with jitter and monitor the result. For validation errors or access-denied responses, don't repeatedly retry the same bad request; fix the input or permissions instead. The lower checklist reinforces the sequence from evidence collection to remediation and verification. One trace may show the failure point, while CloudWatch logs provide application context. Use both to support a concrete fix rather than treating every model error as a generic outage.
